     Ablative CO2 laser treatments use a beam of light to remove the outer layers of the skin, revealing smoother, fresher skin beneath, while also heating deeper layers to stimulate collagen production.   This helps tighten and firm the skin over time. The treatment can be quite intense and likely requires general anesthesia, especially for deeper procedures.   Recovery time can require two weeks or more, but the skin can remain red for several weeks or longer. 
      Nonablative lasers are gentler and allow for quicker recovery. Most nonablative lasers are fractional. This treatment uses a beam of light (laser), divided into thousands of microscopic pixels, and is delivered by a device to treat a small fraction of the skin at a time without damaging the skin's top layer.  There are no serious side effects; typically redness and swelling lasting two days. During the healing process new cells are generated improving skin texture and tone. This type of treatment gets rid of fine lines, age spots, enlarged pores and smoothes textured skin.  Results are achieved with little discomfort and minimal risk, usually after a series of 3-5 treatments, with one treatment every 3-8 weeks.  Downtime is minimal, only a few days at most. It delivers powerful results without the harsh side effects or the high risk of complications posed by ablative laser therapy. This treatment is safe for all skin types.
     If you're considering laser therapy, consult a dermatologist about which option is recommended.

Investing in a new comfortable, durable bike saddle is a great way to upgrade your bicycle and improve your overall cycling experience. Bike saddles come in different lengths, widths, shapes, and rails and there are saddles with memory foam, gel, and some with no padding at all. 

On mountain trails you will probably be in a variety of riding positions. The saddle needs to have sufficient padding for your sit bones, a durable cover, round edges, and a short nose that will allow you to move freely. You also might enjoy a central cutout that reduces pressure on the perineum area. The cut out also improves airflow which reduces moisture and friction. Everything from the padding to the width of the saddle itself is variable. Performance saddles are narrow and long allowing you to have the maximum level of power transfer while you are peddling and the least amount of thigh chafing.

There are three important elements to consider in mountain bike saddles. First, it needs some padding where your sit bones are. The padding can be made from either gel or memory foam. Although gel is cheaper and softer it gets compressed over time. Foam last longer so it's a better long term investment. Second, is a cover that requires little maintenance, should withstand the weather and be slippery enough to assuage chaffing but durable enough to withstand scratches. Third, is the rails. Saddle rails can be made from steel, titanium, or alloy. These materials affect the price and the weight.

Clipless pedals are a popular choice for a casual rider for a smoother ride and are great at giving you more power on each stroke.

label: There is serval different ways to determine if your bike chain is too long or two short. Method #1 General length, on a bike with regular derailleur gears, it should be just long enough to leave some give in the spring of the rear derailleur wen the chainring is on the largest chainring and largest sprocket.  If it is much longer than that then will it be far too loose when in the smaller ring/sprocket combinations and will be likely to bounce off.  For reference a brand-new chin will measure 12 inches across 12 links so if you measure your chain and it is 12 1/16 inches across 12 links then it's time to replace it.  Method # 2 Chain sizing by equation is a common method to determine chain length.  It is possible to determine chain length from a simple equation before you even take a new chain out of the box.  Rember, you can only join the inner plates to the outer plates of a chain, so you can only calculate to the whole inch increments.  L =2 (C) +(F/4+R/4+1) L= Length-your chain length in inches (rounded to the nearest inch). C=Chain stay-the distance between the middle of the crank to the rear axle. Measure to the closest1/8 and convert this to decimal form. F- Front chainring-The number of teeth on the largest (front) chainring. this number is often printed on the sprockets and cogs, but if not, you will have to count.

response: To calculate the correct chain length, start with a chain slightly longer than the big chainring and cassette, then add a full link. This ensures proper tension and avoids tightness, especially when using the largest gears. For accurate results, refer to manufacturer guidelines or use an online calculator to avoid errors. label: There are simple measurements just to check, first to see if your current chain is the correct length.  Shift into the largest chainring and largest cog.  You should be able to make the shift to the largest cog easily.  You should also see two slight bends at each jockey wheel of the rear derailleur.  If the chain is too short, this shift is difficult to make, and the derailleur cage is stretched out and almost parallel to the chainstay. A more precise method includes removing your current chain.   Once the chain has been removed, shift the front derailleur to the largest chainring, and the rear to the smallest. Wrap the chain around the largest chainring (at the rear), making that if the chain has an outer plate, it is routed toward the front chainring.  Pass the chain through the front derailleur cage and onto the largest front chainring, Hold chain at the 5 o’clock position.  If you are using a masterlink chain, install half the mater link onto the front end of the chain to account for the extra half link the master link provides.
